note: Existing-source, strict-license-screened public gallery. Additional historical photos remain held from this site. Anatomy overlays are teaching annotations, not a separate verified voucher determination.

tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — CLUSTERED SPIKELETS
tiles.details: Follow a whole panicle, not just the red color. GrassBase describes panicles ~5–30 cm long, sometimes contracted, with spikelets CLUMPED along branches and short ~0.5–1 mm pedicels. Real Patrick Alexander and Douglas Goldman photographs show flowering clusters; Goldman closeups are source-labelled subsp. oxylepis, not proof of all varieties. Existing gallery panels 0–1 are real mature spikelet clusters; panel 4 is another cluster photograph. Panel 5 is a separate provisionally determined sparse view and should not be treated as verified dense red-lovegrass architecture.
tiles.short: Perennial bunchgrass with chunky multi-flowered spikelets grouped on ascending branches.
tiles.status: SOURCE-LABELLED MATURE CLUSTERS AVAILABLE — FORM AND MEASUREMENT HOLD

tiles.heading: 02 · ROOTED PERENNIAL + SHEATH
tiles.details: Confirm a persistent rooted crown and connected flowering culm. Do not decide perennial versus annual from a detached panicle. GrassBase reports flat or inrolled narrow blades and hairy sheath mouth; these are literature-based dimensions, not measurements from archived gallery pixels. Existing Texas in-soil habit panels 6 (Seadrift) and 7 (Willow Park) show living lower bunches and attached flowering culms, but no exposed fibrous roots or rhizomes. Panels 2–3 and 8 instead show exterior blade–sheath junctions, not roots.
tiles.short: Perennial tuft, flowering culms commonly ~30–75 cm; blades ~2–2.5 mm wide in GrassBase.
tiles.status: IN-SOIL TEXAS BUNCH AND FLOWERING CULMS AVAILABLE — EXPOSED ROOTS STILL NEEDED

tiles.heading: 03 · TRUE LIGULE VERSUS SHEATH-MOUTH HAIRS
tiles.details: Pull the blade away from its sheath and inspect the inner junction at 10–20×. Distinguish actual ligule hairs from the longer outer oral/collar hairs. The existing two Goldman subsp. oxylepis images show the leaf insertion, but NOT a reliably unfolded and measured true fringe; their arrows must not be relabeled 'ligule' without pixel proof. Panel 8 adds a source-identified exterior blade/sheath V from Texas, not an opened free ligule; panels 2–3 remain explicitly subsp. oxylepis. Do not transfer oxylepis-only visual details to all forms.
tiles.short: TRUE ligule is a short fringe of hairs; do not invent a millimeter value.
tiles.status: THREE EXTERIOR COLLAR VIEWS AVAILABLE — FREE INNER LIGULE STILL MISSING

tiles.heading: 04 · MEASURE MATURE SPIKELETS
tiles.details: On one source-vouchered ripe spikelet, photograph both faces with 1-mm scale, count actual stacked florets, and distinguish each floret from the whole spikelet. GrassBase describes disarticulation below individual florets. The existing mature pink-red cluster photos establish gross arrangement, not a reliable measured floret count. Existing panels 0–1 and 4 demonstrate mature stacked florets and clusters without an independent 1-mm calibration; do not re-request another generic clustered flowering head.
tiles.status: MATURE SPIKELET CLUSTERS AVAILABLE — CALIBRATED FLORET COUNT MISSING

tiles.heading: 05 · TWO GLUMES, LEMMA, PALEA AND AWN
tiles.details: Dissect one mature spikelet at 20–40×: both membranous basal glumes are shorter than the spikelet; the lower is ~70–80% the upper. Separate a three-veined red-to-brown fertile lemma and its palea (palea keels may be ciliate). GrassBase describes acute lemma apex, not a long projecting awn. These are published ranges, not proof of microscopic details in the archived photos.
tiles.short: Lower glume ~2.5–3 mm (1 vein), upper ~3–4 mm (1 vein); fertile lemma ~1.6–2.4 mm (3 veins), NO long awn.

tiles.heading: 06 · LOCAL LOOK-ALIKES + PUBLIC-READY GATE
tiles.details: E. spectabilis has widely spreading flexible branches with more dispersed spikelets; E. cilianensis is an introduced ANNUAL with coarser often gland-pitted structures; E. lugens has narrower rolled blades and smaller dispersed spikelets; Tridens texanus may be rosy but has distinct three-veined lemma anatomy. NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO: a Texas-vouchered specimen exposing true roots (existing panels 6–7 show in-soil habit), unfolded measured true inner hair-fringe ligule (panels 2–3,8 are exterior junctions), and 1-mm mature spikelet dissection with both glumes, lemma and palea; a same-scale E. spectabilis comparison (existing panel 9 is unscaled). NEEDS_SITE_QA: check twelve image records, ten teaching panels and eleven existing markers, exact CC0/CC BY/CC BY-SA rights, oxylepis qualifiers, visible arrow endpoints and mobile site rendering. Do not mark FINISHED.
tiles.short: Red color is not enough: compare purple lovegrass, stinkgrass, plains lovegrass and Tridens.
tiles.status: PURPLE LOVEGRASS COMPARISON PANEL 9 — MATCHED ANATOMY AND PUBLIC QA STILL NEEDED

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: Look for the comparatively DENSE panicle: large, many-flowered spikelets packed into clusters along ascending branches. Many can appear rosy-red or violet, but spikelet DENSITY and CLUSTERING are stronger than color. Use a mature isolated spikelet to confirm multiple florets before deciding.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: Start with Patrick Alexander's public-domain photograph of mature pink reddish spikelets. The overlapping scales shown belong to flowering spikelets; don't guess floret or vein count from this view.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: Confirm a persistent rooted crown and connected flowering culm. Do not decide perennial versus annual from a detached panicle. GrassBase reports flat or inrolled narrow blades and hairy sheath mouth; these are literature-based dimensions, not measurements from archived gallery pixels. Existing Texas in-soil habit panels 6 (Seadrift) and 7 (Willow Park) show living lower bunches and attached flowering culms, but no exposed fibrous roots or rhizomes. Panels 2–3 and 8 instead show exterior blade–sheath junctions, not roots.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: Follow a whole panicle, not just the red color. GrassBase describes panicles ~5–30 cm long, sometimes contracted, with spikelets CLUMPED along branches and short ~0.5–1 mm pedicels. Real Patrick Alexander and Douglas Goldman photographs show flowering clusters; Goldman closeups are source-labelled subsp. oxylepis, not proof of all varieties. Existing gallery panels 0–1 are real mature spikelet clusters; panel 4 is another cluster photograph. Panel 5 is a separate provisionally determined sparse view and should not be treated as verified dense red-lovegrass architecture.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: E. spectabilis: open flexible cloud with more separate spikelets; E. cilianensis: annual often with conspicuous craterlike glands along branchlets and lemma keels. E. lugens: narrow inrolled leaves and markedly smaller solitary spikelets; Tridens texanus: do not assume genus from reddish panicle, verify grass spikelet floral details.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

intro: Look for the comparatively DENSE panicle: large, many-flowered spikelets packed into clusters along ascending branches. Many can appear rosy-red or violet, but spikelet DENSITY and CLUSTERING are stronger than color. Use a mature isolated spikelet to confirm multiple florets before deciding.
memory_rule: RED LOVEGRASS = clustered, much chunkier spikelets, typically on ascending branches; purple lovegrass = widely spreading cloud.
safety_note: All four new JPEGs public-safe CC0/CC BY-SA 4.0 and physically read back in GitHub. Two gross-structure arrows added only to obvious photographed spikelet cluster and leaf/sheath insertion. No new claim of visible ligule hair fringe, measured spikelet florets, source Hays locality, or completed Pages/mobile QA.
field_rule: Physical species-recognition evidence: reddish compressed many-flowered spikelets + real leaf sheath/collar, with oxylepis qualification on the Goldman macro references; do not substitute appearance for same-specimen microscopy.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.
comparison_text: E. spectabilis: open flexible cloud with more separate spikelets; E. cilianensis: annual often with conspicuous craterlike glands along branchlets and lemma keels. E. lugens: narrow inrolled leaves and markedly smaller solitary spikelets; Tridens texanus: do not assume genus from reddish panicle, verify grass spikelet floral details.
